query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Implementing a real-time, machine-learning-based feedback control system that adapts laser scanning parameters during L-PBF of AlCrFeNiSi powder will reduce local overheating and compositional fluctuations, thereby lowering residual stress, mitigating segregation, and improving mechanical integrity compared to standard static-parameter fabrication.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi alloy in powder form for laser powder bed fusion.
generation.intervention: Real-time in-process adaptive laser scanning parameter control using machine learning and sensor feedback (e.g., melt-pool monitoring).
generation.conditions: Laser powder bed fusion builds with on-the-fly adjustments to process parameters such as laser power, scan speed, and preheat temperature, within typical industrial ranges (e.g., 50–400 W power, 200–1000 mm/s scan speed).
generation.structural_mediator: Maintaining a stable melt pool and minimizing steep temperature gradients, thus preventing localized over-heating or under-heating.
generation.mechanism: Adaptive control keeps the thermal profile more uniform and shortens the duration of liquid-solid transitions, suppressing segregation and mitigating stress accumulation to enhance mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventionally fabricated samples, the real-time controlled builds will exhibit lower residual stress, reduced porosity and microcracks, and higher tensile strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: AlCrFeNiSi alloy parts processed via conventional quasi-static laser scan parameter settings or cast methods, often exhibiting larger chemical segregation, higher residual stresses, and more defect formation.
generation.boundary: This strategy is expected to hold where accurate, in-situ sensor data can be obtained, and ML algorithms remain well-trained for AlCrFeNiSi powder under typical L-PBF modes. Substantial changes in alloy composition or machine setup may require re-optimization.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in properties and defect mitigation may vary due to machine-to-machine variability, build geometry, sensor noise, and training set completeness; further refinement may be required for large-scale industrial application.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two batches of AlCrFeNiSi samples: one using the real-time ML-based scanning parameter adjustments versus a control batch made via standard static settings. Keep all other parameters constant.
measurements: Elemental mapping to assess compositional uniformity and segregation
Residual stress determination via X-ray diffraction
Defect density via scanning electron microscopy (porosity, microcracks)
Room-temperature tensile testing for yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-controlled samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in defects or residual stress and no improvement in mechanical properties compared to standard processing, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractMany engineering alloys originally designed for conventional manufacturing lack considerations for additive manufacturing (AM), presenting opportunities for novel alloy designs. Evaluating alloy printability requires extensive analysis of chemical composition and processing conditions. The complexity of experimental exploration drives the need for high-throughput computational frameworks. This study introduces a framework that integrates material properties, processing parameters, and melt pool profiles from three thermal models to assess process-induced defects, such as lack-of-fusion, balling, and keyholing. A deep learning surrogate model accelerates the printability assessment by 1000 times without losing accuracy. We validate the framework with printability maps for the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi system and apply it to explore printable alloys in the Co-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ni high-entropy alloy space. Ensemble probabilistic printability maps further provide insights into defect likelihood and uncertainty, enhancing alloy design for AM by efficiently navigating vast design spaces.Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Engineering

These approaches enable more accurate prediction of phase formation and mechanical properties, guiding alloy design and reducing experimental trial and error. They reported intergranular hot cracks and high residual stresses in the near vicinity of these cracks. They also showed that hot-cracking susceptibility increases with large, columnar grains and described this behavior with Rappaz-Drezet-Gremaud criterion. Many scholars have studied HEAs [,,], but most focus on design principles, metallurgical mechanisms, phase changes, micro-structures, and properties of HEAs manufactured by conventional technologies. Several AM methods have been successfully implemented to fabricate structures with HEAs []. The powder bed fusion (PBF) processes, specifically the selected laser melting (SLM) technique, have been widely adopted []. SLM is a powder-bed additive manufacturing technology, which is also advantageous for producing complex-shaped parts []. During the SLM process, rapid melting and solidification are attributable to short-time interaction between laser energy and metal powder, which facilitates the formation of fine microstructure and improves the mechanical properties of the parts []. Meanwhile, ultra-fast cooling helps prevent the formation of intermetallic compounds and element dissolution. Thus, SLM was recently also used for HEA manufacturing, and some studies on the manufacturing, microstructure, and tensile properties of these alloys have been reported []. decision.trend: Early work (PMC6427779, 2019) used selective laser melting (SLM) of refractory high-entropy alloys while noting that large density and thermal gradients could lead to composition deviations. Subsequent efforts (PMC8201384, 2021) demonstrated near-complete fusion and high density (≈99.8%) via careful in-situ alloy formation and parameter tuning. Later studies (PMC9698306, 2022; PMC9736672, 2022) on other multi-principal element alloys used laser powder-bed fusion or SLM process optimization (e.g., adjusting laser energy densities) to limit defects and refine microstructures, although stress accumulation and localized segregation remained concerns. More recent work (PMC11822122, 2025) exploited a metastable phase approach to tune the microstructure during additive manufacturing, but controlling grain size, residual stress, and chemical uniformity simultaneously is still challenging. Most recently (PMC12250662, 2025), investigations into laser powder bed fusion of Co-based HEAs revealed hot-cracking risks at high energy densities, reinforcing the need for temperature-gradient minimization and in-process control strategies. Despite progress, achieving robust mechanical integrity without segregation or stress-related defects remains an open challenge when fabricating cobalt-free HEAs such as AlCrFeNiSi.
decision.unsolved: No single method fully reconciles the trade-offs among minimal segregation, low residual stress, and defect suppression for cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi. Traditional bulk routes risk compositional segregation during solidification, while standard additive approaches incur considerable thermal gradients, leading to micro-cracking and distortion. A technique that jointly manages composition uniformity and mechanical properties, without relying on additional alloying, has yet to be established.
decision.lever: Implement real-time, machine-learning-based control of laser scanning parameters (e.g., power, spot speed, preheat temperature) for an in-process feedback loop, adjusting these parameters on the fly to maintain reduced thermal gradients and minimize solidification segregation in AlCrFeNiSi powder bed fusion builds.
decision.why: Prior studies identify thermal gradients, localized overheating, and associated microstructural non-uniformities as key drivers of stress concentrations, defects, and segregation in high-entropy alloys. A closed-loop machine-learning approach can incorporate melt-pool monitoring data, predict incipient stresses, and adapt process settings to ensure more uniform cooling and composition, thus addressing the persistent trade-offs of structural integrity, segregation, and defect mitigation without altering alloy chemistry.
